title: Ethereum whale's $13.45M loss reflects a year-long exit, not a fresh ETH dump
body: Ethereum whale's $13.45 million loss is a year-long exit, not a fresh dump A wallet that began buying Ethereum (ETH) near last year's market peak has now moved almost its entire position onto exchanges. On-chain analyst Ai Yi flagged the activity, Odaily reported it, and Binance News carried it on Friday. The headline figure, a potential $13.45 million loss on 15,361 ETH, checks out arithmetically. But it describes twelve months of activity, not a single sale this week, and that difference matters for how traders should read it. What the wallet actually did The investor started buying in September 2025 at around $4,600 and kept adding as prices fell. In total, 15,810 ETH was withdrawn from exchanges at an average cost of about $4,100, roughly $65 million. Between October 2025 and October 2026, the wallet sent 15,361 ETH back to exchanges at an average price of about $3,226. The most recent deposit came a few hours before the report, but its size was not disclosed. The wallet still holds 572 ETH. Why a deposit is not the same as a sale Moving coins onto an exchange often comes before selling, which is why analysts track these transfers. But on-chain data shows that coins moved, not that they were sold. Exchange deposits can also be used as collateral for borrowing or for internal transfers. The $13.45 million figure is therefore an estimate. It assumes every deposited coin was sold at the market price on the day it arrived.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6947 – Reuters estimate
body: The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The rejection this week at 5.30% following the US CPI report stands out rather clearly, with yields failing to sustain a break higher before retreating sharply. And that now puts the spotlight back on the 5.00% level, which had previously played the role in keeping yields from breaking out back in September. title: Felix Nikolas Prehn on mortgage rates and the 10-year Treasury yield
body: Felix Nikolas Prehn is an economist and former investment banker whose research examines money, asset prices and US households from 2000 to 2026. A buyer who opens a mortgage quote is looking at the last link in a chain that starts in the bond market. The starting point for a mortgage rate A St. Louis Fed explainer on mortgage rates names the 10-year Treasury note as the benchmark for the 30-year mortgage. Treasury securities count as very low risk because the US government backs them, so investors use their yields as the yardstick for other long-term investments. The choice of a 10-year note for a 30-year loan comes down to how long people keep their mortgages. Many are written for 30 years, but most are paid off, refinanced or ended by the sale of the home well before then. The average life of a mortgage is much closer to 10 years. Some banks bundle thousands of mortgages into securities and sell them to investors, who receive the principal and interest homeowners pay. Those investors compare the return on mortgage-backed securities with the return on the 10-year note. The two respond to the same signals, such as data on inflation and economic growth, and their yields often move in the same direction. The securities are riskier than Treasuries, so investors demand a higher yield for taking that risk. The explainer calls the market value of that extra risk, plus the added costs of a mortgage (origination expenses, servicing fees and lender profit), the mortgage spread.

title: Where do traders get interest rate expectations for central banks?
body: Interest rate expectations are among the most important drivers for financial markets. They influence government bond yields, currencies, equity valuations, and even cryptocurrencies. But how can traders check whether the market expects a central bank to cut rates, hold them steady, or deliver rate hikes? The answer lies in interest rate derivatives, particularly overnight index swaps (OIS) and interest rate futures. These instruments allow market participants to express views on future interest rates, hedge their exposure to changes in monetary policy, and translate market prices into implied expectations. The market doesn't wait for a central bank meeting to form expectations about its next decision. Traders can buy and sell derivatives whose value depends on interest rates over specific future periods. When macro or geopolitical developments change the future outlook, or central bank officials communication hints to a certain decision, traders reassess the likely path of monetary policy before the central bank takes action. They then adjust their positions in interest rate derivatives, causing prices to move. These price movements can be translated into implied interest rates. By comparing the implied rate with the current policy rate, traders can estimate how much tightening or easing the market has priced in. There are two main instruments for this purpose: overnight index swaps and interest rate futures.

title: Germany 10-Year Bund Yield Holds Near 5-Week Low
body: The German 10-year Bund yield was little changed at around 3.42%, hovering near a five-week low, and was down nearly 7 bps for the week. The move tracked a global decline in borrowing costs as expectations for further monetary policy tightening eased. Remarks by Fed Chair Warsh at the IMF summit were widely interpreted as signaling that the Federal Reserve is likely to keep rates unchanged this month, despite inflation data coming in hotter than expected. In Europe, comments from ECB President Lagarde supported a cautious, wait-and-see stance. Lagarde noted that elevated inflation in the Eurozone has been driven "predominantly, but not exclusively" by a surge in energy prices following the Iran war.
